## 1. Your question

1. What environmental question are you curious about? State it in one sentence.
- Is the amount of avalanche related fatalities in California positively correlates with El Nino cycles of ENSO?\ 

2. Why does this question matter, and to whom? Who would make a different decision depending on the answer?
This question matters a lot. Last year Mammoth Mountain was not prepared for the amount of snowfall that they received, and it costed them the lives of several ski patrolers, skiers, and millions of dollars. It was a La Nina phase-- notorious for less snowfall than an El Nino phase. THis year is the strongest El Nino of all time, which may lead to several casualties if not aptly prepared. The average skier may not want to ski with a greater risk of avalanche fatalities, whereas a resort owner may increase their survailanece and field testing due to this data.\ 

3. What do you already know about this topic? Name at least one source (e.g., a paper, report, or news article) that gives context for your question.
[This article](https://abc7news.com/post/final-report-deadly-castle-peak-avalanche-lake-tahoe-details-snow-conditions-movements-9-victims/18832449/) talks about the scieence behind how snow droughts cause worse snowpack when storms finally arrive. As a geographer, I am aware of current ENSO conditions and am familiar with what that means in terms of snowpac. LA a Nina brought a snow drought for most of America, but this years record breaking El Nino will break that drought-- and lead to dangerous snowpack.\ 

4. What is your **response** variable? What is the main **explanatory** variable you think influences it?\ 
The response variable is avalanche incidents ending in fatalities. They are caused by bad snowpack (among other avoidable factors), which are a direct consequence of ENSO storm regimes.\ 

## 2. Your data

1. What dataset(s) will you use to answer your question? Provide the source and a link.
- For avalanche data I will be using [Colorado Avalance Information Center](https://avalanche.state.co.us/accidents/statistics-and-reporting) publicly available avalance incident data.
- For El Nino data, I will be using [Niño 3.4 SST Index from the HadISST1.1](https://psl.noaa.gov/data/timeseries/month/DS/Nino34/). I will be looking at the sea surface temperature anomaly in the Nino 3.4 region.

2. Who collected these data, how, and why? How might the way the data were collected affect what you can learn from them?

- For the avalanche data, all of the incident data are reports. The data comes from all around the country and from several sources. Data is reported this way because indiviuals caught in an avalance report their incidents for future safety, and rescue teams who report this data do so to keep a record of incidents in their area. A lot of the time there are avalanche fatalities that dont got reported because there were no survivors and people were far in the backcountry-- especially in earlier years when SOS technolgy was less advanced. This may cause underreporting of hazardous conditions.\ 
- The ONI data is a collection of several sources such as boat thermisters, CTD buoys, and satelite derived data. Because the data is coming from several different sources over a long period of time, there may be inconsistencies in the data. Thermal remote sensing has come a long way since the 70s. The anomaly is a harmonic composition of these different data sources, which varies with season.\ 

3. What does one row in your data represent (e.g., one site, one year, one sample)? How many rows are there?
- For the avalanche center data, one row in the data represents one reported avalanche incident and all of its related information. One row essentially represents one incident report.\ 
- For the el nino data, one row represents the sea surface temperature anomaly for the first day of that month in the nino 3.4 region.

4. Download the data and read it into R. Include the code for cleaning your data, or joining it if you have multiple sources.
```{r}
# Read in libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(readxl)

# Read in data and do basic cleaning
avalanche_CA_data <- read_excel(here("eds222-finalproj", "data", "CAIC_Accident_Data_Oct_2025.xlsx")) |> 
    filter(State == 'CA') 

nino_data <- read_csv(here("eds222-finalproj", "data", "nino34.long.anom.csv"))
colnames(nino_data) <- c("date", "sst_anomaly")

avalanche_CA_data |> head(1)
nino_data |> head(1)
```

## 4. Graphical summaries
- We need to clean the data a little bit more before we can start plotting, because the -9999 values will throw off our graph scale.
```{r}
nino_data$sst_anomaly[nino_data$sst_anomaly == -9999] <- NA
nino_data$sst_anomaly |>  is.na() |> sum()
```

1. Visualize the **distribution** of your response variable. Describe its shape (e.g., symmetric, skewed, bounded by zero).
- Visualizse the temporal distribution of avalanches in California via the database
```{r}
avalanche_CA_data |> 
    ggplot(
        mapping = aes(
            x=Date,
            y=Killed
            
        )
    ) +
    geom_line() +
    labs(
        x='Date of Incident',
        y='Number of Fatalities',
        title='California Avalanche Incident Distribution Time Series'
    ) +
        theme_classic()
```
This chart shows the annual distribution of California avalanches *from this database* on a decadal scale. It is clear that around 1980 had the mos t
2. Visualize the **relationship** between your response and explanatory variables. Describe what you see.

```{r}
avy_year <- avalanche_CA_data |> 
    summarize(year_count = sum(Killed), .by = YYYY) |> 
    rename(year = YYYY)
chart2_df <- nino_data |> 
    mutate(year = year(date)) |> 
    summarize(mean_sst = mean(sst_anomaly), .by = year) |> 
    inner_join(avy_year, by = join_by(year)) |> 
    ggplot(
        mapping = aes(
            x=year
        )
    ) +
        geom_line(aes(y = mean_sst, color = 'blue')) +
        geom_line(aes(y = year_count, color = 'red')) + 
            labs(
            x= 'Year',
            y = 'Mean sst and Avalanche Fatalities Trend',
            title = "California Avalanche Incident vs Mean sst Over Time",
            color = "Legend Color"
        )  +
        scale_color_discrete(labels = c("blue" = "Mean SST Anomaly (celsius)", 
                                  "red" = "Fatality Count"))

        chart2_df
``` 
The relatioship between avalanche fatalies ad mean sea surface temperature anomaly is displayed on the chart in a decadal scale. Around 1980 there are peaks in both graphs, hinting at the idea that there may be a relationship between these two variables.

3. Make at least one more figure that shows something about your data you think is important (e.g., variation over space or time, differences between groups, a potential confounding variable).

Every figure should have informative axis labels with units and a caption explaining what it shows.

I am going to repeat the same analysis as seen above, however I am going to change the data so that it displays aalanche incidents that happened in Colorado. I want to see if a similar relationship can be obsevred. El Nino affects the weather pattersns much differently in Colorado as supposed to the Sierras.
```{r}
avalanche_CO_data <- read_excel(here("eds222-finalproj", "data", "CAIC_Accident_Data_Oct_2025.xlsx")) |> 
    filter(State == 'CO')
avy_year_CO <- avalanche_CO_data |> 
    summarize(year_count = sum(Killed), .by = YYYY) |> 
    rename(year = YYYY)
chart2_df <- nino_data |> 
    mutate(year = year(date)) |> 
    summarize(mean_sst = mean(sst_anomaly), .by = year) |> 
    inner_join(avy_year_CO, by = join_by(year)) |> 
    ggplot(
        mapping = aes(
            x=year
        )
    ) +
        geom_line(aes(y = mean_sst, color = 'blue')) +
        geom_line(aes(y = year_count, color = 'red')) + 
            labs(
            x= 'Year',
            y = 'Mean sst and Avalanche Fatalities Trend',
            title = "Colorado Avalanche Incident vs Mean sst Over Time",
            color = "Legend Color"
        )  +
        scale_color_discrete(labels = c("blue" = "Mean SST Anomaly (celsius)", 
                                  "red" = "Fatality Count"))

        chart2_df
```
A different trend is observed in this data. As the years pass there seems to be an upward, decadal, trend in avalanche fatalities. Further analysis about this relationship would have to be completed in order to discern whether or not this trend is statistically significant.
